stem: A HIV carrier with ring-like lesions on MRI scan is most likely to have a diagnosis of:
explanation: Cerebral toxoplasmosis commonly affects patients with advanced HIV immunodeficiency. Toxoplasmosis with CNS involvement in patients who are immunocompromised can be severe and debilitating, and the condition may be fatal. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scan shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions with extensive surrounding oedema in supratentorial as well as the infratentorial region.

stem: Which one of the following tests would be best used for testing executive function?
explanation:
The Trail Making Test (TMT) has two parts and the times taken to complete each part are used to measure central executive functioning. In Part A, the participant must draw a line to connect consecutive numbers, 1 to 25. This

tests visual screening, processing speed, attention. In Part B the participant connects numbers and letters in an alternating progressive sequence (i.e. connect A-1-B-2-C-3 and so on). This tests central executive processes of task-set inhibition, cognitive flexibility, and the ability to maintain a response set. In order to measure central executive functioning, the difference in time taken to complete TMT-B and TMT-A (which has little executive input) is calculated.

stem: A doctor, during a clinical interview, tells a patient, "I think I now have a good idea of your financial situation; perhaps we should talk about your family problems now". Which technique is the doctor utilising?
explanation: Transition is an interview technique used when moving from one to another topic. It is a very useful interview skill and preferably must be done as smoothly as possible to keep the patient interested.

stem: What is the most common finding in a newly diagnosed patient with Parkinson's disease?
explanation: Unilateral resting tremor is the most common presenting feature in Parkinson's disease.
reference: Adler and Ahlskog: Parkinson's disease and movement disorders Pg 72

stem: A patient is suspected to have temporal lobe damage resulting from a vascular lesion. Which of the following visual signs may be elicited on perimetry?
explanation: Temporal lesions produce upper quadrantanopia due to damage to optic radiation.

stem: A patient breaks down and cries during interview. Which of the following technique is useful at this stage?
options: Ask a question with multiple choices
explanation: Validation statements facilitate the continuation of a clinical interview by 'normalising' experiences e.g. 'it is normal to cry at difficult times.'

stem: Mr. Y has a diagnosis of chronic schizophrenia. He has polyuria, polydipsia and becomes acutely confused. On further investigation, his serum sodium levels are notably low. What do you suspect?
explanation: Water intoxication occurs particularly in patients with chronic schizophrenia. The clinical presentation includes polyuria, polydipsia, hyponatraemia, confusion, seizures, cerebral and peripheral edema. Death can occur in extreme cases. The cause is generally unknown.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of late-onset schizophrenia?
options: Family history of schizophrenia is infrequent when compared to early onset
White matter hyperintensities on MRI brain
correctAnswer: White matter hyperintensities on MRI brain
explanation:
Late-onset schizophrenia is characterised by:

a predominance of females

fewer negative symptoms

infrequent formal thought disorder

prominent hallucinations (notably visual)

Associations include:

social isolation

sensory impairment

premorbid paranoid personality traits.

Family loading for schizophrenia is lower than for early-onset cases (Howard et al., 2000). White matter hyperintensities are not associated with late-onset schizophrenia (Howard 1995; Rivkin 2000) though one contradictory study exists favouring higher frequency of WMH in late-onset schizophrenia (Sachdev 1999).

stem: A 44-year-old man with schizophrenia has intense suspiciousness and persecutory delusions. He tells you that his neighbours want him to prepare a home-made explosive with detonators. Which of the following would be the best response at this point of interview?
options: Perhaps we should ask your neighbours if this is true
Why do you think your neighbours want you to do that?
No, I don't think this sort of thing could happen
If you prepare explosives, we may have to involve the police
It doesn't sound like a good idea to prepare explosives
correctAnswer: Why do you think your neighbours want you to do that?
explanation: The main purpose of the interview is to collect clinically useful information that will enable diagnostic process and facilitate management. It is important to maintain a good therapeutic relationship with the patient while pursuing the above goals. Enquiring 'Why do you think your neighbours want you to do that?' serves both these purposes.

stem: Obsessions can also occur as
explanation: Obsessions often manifest as intrusive, unwanted thoughts, impulses or 'mental images' of committing an act that the subject considers to be harmful, violent, immoral, sexually inappropriate, or sacrilegious

stem: A 67-year-old male admitted to A and E, when asked what the month was, replied 'January' and when asked what the year was, replied 'January' again. He is exhibiting
explanation:
Perseveration refers to repeatedly same response - either verbal or motor, when different

stimuli are delivered (questions or instructions). Irrespective of changes in stimuli which demand variation in responses, the response remains the same. It is different from Verbigeration where verbal repetition occurs spontaneously, not just in response to questions or commands. Also, note that perseverative responses are goal directed - they intend to answer a question or carry out an instruction, but stereotypes on other hand are not goal directed.

stem: A patient with schizophrenia often rocks back and forth. He is also observed to be thumping his head with his fist for no apparent reason. He is exhibiting which of the following symptoms?
explanation: This patient is demonstrating stereotypy; a symptom characterised by repetitive, functionless motor behaviour. Stereotypies, mannerisms, and verbigeration are often elicited in patients with catatonic schizophrenia. Hemiballism – hyperkinetic movement disorder characterised by violent involuntary proximal limb movements on one side of the body, caused by damage to the subthalamic nucleus of the basal ganglia. Unrelated to schizophrenia. Ambitendency – a motor symptom where a patient who has been given an instruction alternates between automatic obedience and negativism e.g. when asked to shake hands, the patient appears indecisive, repeatedly extending and withdrawing their hand. Ambivalence - described by Bleuler as one of the four primary symptoms of schizophrenia and was defined as having positive and negative emotions at the same time. Patients exhibiting ambivalence often have an inability to decide on an action. Mannerisms - repetitive, goal-directed movements (e.g. saluting).

stem: A patient that you see in your hospital corridor is moving his closed fist round to the right and round to the left in a repetitive manner. He is exhibiting:
explanation: Repetitive, non-goal-directed motor activity (e.g. finger-play, repeatedly touching, patting or rubbing self) is called stereotypy. It is an abnormality not inherent in act but in its frequency.

stem: A man using mescaline 'smelt the noise of the trumpet'. This condition is known as:
explanation: This is a classical example of synaesthesia described by Sims. The phenomenon of perceiving a stimulus of one modality in a different modality (may be single or multiple modalities) is called synaesthesia. E.g. tasting the music, hearing colours and smelling voices. It is not a hallucination as the perceived object has an appropriate stimulus. Reflex hallucinations are a hallucinatory form of synaesthesia. A stimulus in one modality produces a hallucination in another modality.

stem: A psychologist asked Mr. Snowden whether he had any special powers or abilities that other people do not have. He replied that he wasn't sure as he never visited Russia. When asked to clarify, he asked, "If you throw twenty-and-two blackbirds, would you know where does the evening start?" This form of speech is called:
explanation: Tangentiality - speech is organised, but not goal directed. The subject answers a question in an indirect manner with vague relevance. The answer appears distant and drifted away from the original goal.

stem: In psychopathology, the term 'moria' refers to:
options: Tendency to choke when drinking fluids
Tendency to be restless and hyperactive
explanation: Puerile, childish, frivolous, or silly behaviour occurs with right frontotemporal lesions and in frontotemporal dementia. In such cases, moria (foolish or silly euphoria) and Witzelsucht (a tendency to tell inappropriate jokes are seen).

stem: All are true regarding compulsions except
options: Compulsive acts often provoke further anxiety
They are always preceded by an obsessive thought
Washing is the most frequent compulsion
Can be an unobservable mental act
correctAnswer: They are always preceded by an obsessive thought
explanation: Compulsions need not be always preceded by obsessive thoughts; they can be preceded by obsessive images, words or impulses. In some cases of autism, Asperger's syndrome or frontotemporal dementia, compulsive behaviours are noted without any preceding obsessions.

stem: A man complains of repeated thoughts about self-harm. Which of the following is characteristic of obsessions?
options: These thoughts can be stopped at will
explanation: Obsessions are recurrent and stereotyped - i.e. the thoughts occur without much change in their presentation

stem: While examining the mental state of a 47-year-old man with psychosis, you noticed a sudden stop in the flow of his thoughts. This phenomenon can be termed as
explanation: Thought block is a symptom of schizophrenic thought disorder where the patient experiences a sudden break in the chain of thought.

stem: A 35 year old lady in your inpatient unit covers her head with a veil. She claims that other people can hear what she thinks. The most likely description is
explanation:
This lady is experiencing an intrusion into the privacy of her thoughts and others come to

know them 'as she is thinking'. Thought broadcast is generally described as a unique phenomenon where, in a fashion similar to the live (radio or television) telecast of events, one's thoughts appear to get diffuse or broadcasted to others. Another school of thought suggests using this term when patients believe others can hear their thoughts as a consequence of the thought echo phenomenon (where patients themselves can hear their own thoughts). Pawar A and Spence S. Defining Thought Broadcast.The British Journal of Psychiatry (2003) 183: 287-291

stem: Which one of the following is not a characteristic sign in a catatonic patient?
explanation: The characteristic signs seen in a catatonic patient includes posturing, rigidity, staring, mutism, negativism, echolalia and echopraxia.The typical forms include excited or delirious and stuporous or retarded.

stem: A senseless repetition of words is known as
explanation: Verbigeration refers to senseless repetition of sound, words or phrases

stem: The most common modality of illusions is
explanation: The most common modality of illusions is visual. Illusions themselves are not indicative of any psychopathology

stem: The concept of autochthonus idea was formulated by:
explanation: Wernicke described autochthonous ('spontaneous, indigenous, not from any secondary source, out of blue') ideas.

stem: What defense mechanisms are commonly employed by patients with borderline personality disorder?
explanation: Functionally, patients with borderline personality disorder distort their relationships by considering each person to be either all good or all bad. They see people as either nurturing attachment figures or as hateful, sadistic figures who deprive them of security needs and threaten them with abandonment whenever they feel dependent. As a result of this splitting, the good person is idealised and the bad person devalued. Projective identification is another defense mechanism that often occurs in patients with borderline personality disorder. In this primitive defense mechanism, the patient projects intolerable aspects of themselves onto another person, inducing them to play the projected role, and the two persons act in unison.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 564.

stem: A 34 year old man who has a significant conflict with his partner has the following thoughts in the unconscious and the conscious level. I hate him (unconscious); I love him (conscious). This refers to which of the following defense mechanisms?
explanation: Reaction formation involves externally expressing attitudes and behaviours that are the opposite of the unacceptable internal impulses (e.g. being extra polite to a person to avoid expressing anger towards them). Thus, in reaction formation, 'I hate him' becomes 'I love him.'
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 893.

stem: Which of the following can be considered as a neurotic defence mechanism?
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 892-893. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1066-1067.

stem: You arrived late to a psychotherapy meeting and the therapist talks about 'Loss of ego boundaries'. Which of the following condition is she most likely referring to?
explanation: Patients with schizophrenia often experience their ‘self’ as disembodied, and they feel empty, unreal, dead, and differentiated from the world. They are unable to sustain a sense of self as persons, which is why they are equally unable to experience neither separateness from nor relatedness to others in a usual way. They may fear losing their identity in a relationship as well as feel dependent on the other for their very being. The capacity for reality testing and the relative intact ego boundaries in patients with borderline personality organisation are what delimit these patients from the psychoses.
reference: Zandersen M, Parnas J. Identity disturbance, feelings of emptiness, and the boundaries of the schizophrenia spectrum. Schizophrenia Bulletin. 2019 Jan 1;45(1):106-13.

stem: Which of the following is a mature defence mechanism?
explanation: Sublimation is a mature defence, together with humour, suppression, anticipation and altruism.

stem: The term 'Dream Work' described by Sigmund Freud involves
options: Multiple images in dreams represent one unconscious impulse
Transforming latent content into manifest content
Transfer of energy from an original object to a symbolic representation of the object
Several unconscious impulses are combined into a single images
correctAnswer: Transforming latent content into manifest content
explanation: Freud distinguished two types/layers of dream content. Manifest Content refers to what is recalled by the dreamer; Latent Content refers to unconscious thoughts and wishes that threaten to awaken the dreamer. The unconscious mental operation by which the Latent Content is transformed into Manifest Content is called the Dream Work.

stem: There is no processing involved in which of the following types of memory?
explanation: Sensory memory: This is modality specific, has a large capacity but gets disrupted by an inflow of new information in the same modality. Each sense has its own sensory memory e.g. iconic (visual), echoic (auditory). Iconic lasts for 0.5 seconds while echoic lasts for 2 seconds. No processing is involved in sensory memory. Information that is attended to is transferred to short-term memory store, and information that is not selected for processing is rapidly lost.

stem: All are examples of secondary drive except
explanation: Drives refer to purposeful activity initially produced to satisfy an internal need. Drives are commonly divided into primary and secondary drives. Examples of primary drives are eating, drinking, sex. Examples of secondary drives are affection, comfort, achievement, dominance and socialisation. The secondary drives acquire their values through their association with primary drives and often through a social learning process.

stem: A child received generous praise from her parents every time when she wrote a letter of the alphabet. She was praised more when she managed to write a full word. She was rewarded more generously when she wrote a sentence. Which of the following reinforcement is taking place?
explanation: Shaping is an operant conditioning method for producing an entirely new behaviour by using rewards to guide an organism toward a desired behaviour (called 'successive approximations'). The organism is rewarded with each small advancement in the right direction.

stem: Which of the following is one of the maladaptive traits that can be used to further describe a diagnosis of personality disorder in ICD-11?
explanation: The maladaptive traits that can be used to describe a diagnosis of personality disorder in ICD-11 are: negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition and anankastia. A further qualifier of 'borderline pattern' can also be used.

stem: Lucy is learning to write. Her father praises her for holding the pencil correctly, then for scribbling something on a piece of paper and writing something vaguely which resembles like a letter. The learning theory principle employed here is:
explanation:
Shaping is a teaching technique by which a child is rewarded for a successful approximation of a target skill. If a child is learning to write his or her name, say "Alex," a teacher would

shape the responses by starting with the letter A and providing the other letters: _lex. The next step would be perhaps for the child to write the first and last letters independently. The process would continue until the child can write his name independently. (Webster J, 2008. Retrieved from http://specialed.about.com/od/glossary/g/shaping.htm)

stem: Which of the following concepts is reflective of a change in ICD-11 (from ICD-10)?
options: Use of dimensional approach for all disorders
Removal of minimum symptom count for all disorders
Introduction of gender incongruence as mental health disorder
All disorders can be diagnosed at any age
correctAnswer: All disorders can be diagnosed at any age
explanation: ICD-11 takes a lifespan approach to diagnosis, permitting diagnoses which were usually associated with childhood or adolescence, such as attachment or conduct disorder, to be diagnosed at any age. It specifically considers the cultural background of a patient in diagnosis. A dimensional approach has been taken in personality and primary psychotic disorders, as well as for depressive episodes in mood disorders. Minimum symptom counts have been removed from diagnostic criteria for most disorders, but not major depression. Gender incongruence, replacing gender identity disorder, has been moved to the sexual health chapter of ICD-11 as it is not a mental health disorder.

stem: Who proposed the two-factor theory of intelligence?
explanation: The two-factor theory of intelligence was postulated by Spearman. Spearman carried out a factor analysis of the result of children's performance on a number of tests and concluded that all tests measured both a common factor of general intelligence (g) and a specific factor (s). He believed that individual differences were due to differences in (g). According to Sternberg, component intelligence is used for executive tasks and experiential intelligence is used for routine tasks that have already been learnt or mastered.

stem: A 44 year old woman is terrified of heights. She develops a sense of vertigo even at 1st or 2nd floor of a building and avoids high rise buildings at all cost. The company she is working for undergoes relocation and she is required now to work at 15th floor of a building in central London. Which of the following is the best treatment option for her?
explanation: Simple phobias such as acrophobia can be treated with the behavioural technique of systematic desensitisation. Systematic desensitisation is based on the behavioural principle of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). It involves three steps: relaxation training, constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and desensitisation of the stimulus. The patient is exposed to a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking situations in stepwise fashion while being taught to practice the relaxation techniques (e.g. a young woman with a spider phobia is taught relaxation techniques and then exposed to experiences starting from the lowest level of her hierarchy of anxieties - such as going to the cellar where there is the potential to come across a spider - then progressively going up the ladder to the highest - such as handling a spider).
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

stem: A 40-year-old man who works for the state as a highway and bridge designer becomes extremely anxious when he has to drive across any bridge. Which technique can best help him?
explanation: Systematic desensitisation can reduce anxiety in a situation by identifying a hierarchy of situations that produce anxiety from low to high. For example, the bridge designer can be taught progressive muscle relaxation until he is as relaxed as possible, at which point he will begin by driving across the shortest or least anxiety-producing bridge (in vivo exposure). As he successfully experiences crossing the lowest anxiety-producing bridge, he can proceed up the hierarchy of bridges until he masters crossing the most anxiety-producing bridge. Systematic desensitisation is based on the behavioural principle of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). It involves three steps: relaxation training, constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and desensitisation of the stimulus. The patient is exposed to a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking situations in stepwise fashion while being taught to practice the relaxation techniques.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

stem: A psychiatrist shows several pictures to encourage her patient to narrate imaginative stories and descriptions. On the basis of the responses, she makes an assessment of the patient's personality. Which of the following best describes this test?
explanation: The thematic apperception test is a projective personality test. It consists of a series of 10 black-and-white pictures that depict individuals of both sexes and of different age groups, who are involved in a variety of different activities. The stories that the patient makes up concerning the pictures, according to the projective hypothesis, reflect the patient’s own needs, thoughts, feelings, stresses, wishes, desires, and views of the future.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 59-60.

stem: According to Eysenck's three-factor theory which of the following is a feature of an extraverted person?
options: They have a less reactive reticular activating system
They have an overactive reticular activating system
They have a high autonomic lability
correctAnswer: They have a less reactive reticular activating system
explanation: Eysenck believed that differences in extraversion were due to physiological differences in brain systems that caused some people to be more easily aroused than others. Specifically, he proposed that the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) regulated arousal. People differ in the sensitivity of this system, which causes them to respond differently to their environment. A moderately stimulating environment might cause people with a very sensitive ARAS to feel overstimulated and retreat (i.e., to behave like introverts), but people with a less sensitive ARAS to feel under-stimulated and seek out additional stimulation (i.e., to behave like extraverts).
reference: Caroline Fielden et al. Extraversion. James D. Wright (Ed). International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences (Second Edition), Elsevier, 2015, 623-27.

stem: Recalling an address with three items tests which one of the following?
explanation: Verbal memory refers to the memory of words and other abstractions involving language

stem: A 39-year-old man can be tested for current IQ using
explanation: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scales are for people aged 16 and over.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 82.

stem: Which of the following determines one's cultural identity?
explanation: Race is perceived as a permanent entity determined by genetic ancestry and characterised by physical appearance. Culture is perceived as a changeable entity determined by upbringing and choice and characterised by behaviours and attitudes. Ethnicity is perceived as partially changeable entity determined by social pressure and psychological need characterised by a sense of group identity and belonging. (Ref: Seminars in General Adult Psychiatry, RCPsych Gaskell Press, Pg 783.)

stem: Which of the following is a new mental health disorder under ICD-11?
explanation:
Prolonged grief disorder is a new mental health disorder under ICD-11 categorised under disorders specifically associated with stress. It describes a persistent and disabling grief reaction, which lasts longer than 6 months and is out of keeping with what is expected for the

cultural context. ‘Trichotillomania’ was in ICD-10, as was hyperkinetic disorder, which has now been re- categorised as ADHD. Sadomasochism and other consensual sexual practices are no longer generally considered to be pathological. ‘Acute stress reaction’ is no longer seen as a mental health condition, but as a normal reaction to extreme stress. It is categorised under factors influencing health status or contact with health services.

stem: William Tuke's approach to the treatment of insanity was called
explanation: William Tuke was a 19 th century reformist and philanthropist notable for his work in mental health. He was known for his strict self-discipline and judicious manner and was a firm believer in the Quaker faith. Possibly catalysed by the very public mismanagement of King George III’s ‘madness’, he pioneered the use of moral treatment, a humane method of treating mental illness. This focused on allowing patients to live in a community, partake in daily activities, and not be subjected to the brutality of the commonplace asylum. Tuke went on to aid in the reform of the law with regards to asylums.
reference: Kibria AA, Metcalfe NH. A biography of William Tuke (1732–1822): Founder of the modern mental asylum. Journal of medical biography. 2016 Aug;24(3):384-8.

stem: The term stigma was first popularised by
explanation: Stigma is a mark of disgrace associated with a person, a personal quality, or a personal circumstance. In ancient Greece, bodily signs were sometimes cut or burnt into the bodies of people to advertise their status as slaves, criminal, or traitors and to indicate that they were blemished, ritually polluted, and to be avoided, especially in public places. The term was introduced into the social sciences by sociologist Erving Goffman in a book entitled Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

stem: A psychosomatic family process has been described in association with eating disorders. The features of such a psychosomatic family includes
explanation: Minuchin and colleagues defined predominant characteristics of families with an anorectic adolescent (so-called ‘psychosomatic families’), including enmeshment, rigidity, insufficient conflict resolution skills, and overprotectiveness.
reference: Herpertz-Dahlmann B et al. Aetiology of anorexia nervosa: from a “psychosomatic family model” to a neuropsychiatric disorder?. European archives of psychiatry and clinical neuroscience. 2011 Nov;261(2):177-81.

stem: Select the correct statement regarding schizophrenia in African-Caribbean population
options: Second generation African-Caribbeans with schizophrenia are more likely to develop
An increased rate of schizophrenia is not found in Jamaica, the country of origin for most African-Caribbeans in the UK.
The rate of prescription of depot medications for second generation African-Caribbeans
in the UK are the same as that of Caucasian subjects
Second generation African-Caribbeans with Schizophrenia are more likely to have a
The first admission rates for second generation African-Caribbeans in the UK are the
same as that of Caucasian subjects
correctAnswer: An increased rate of schizophrenia is not found in Jamaica, the country of origin for most African-Caribbeans in the UK.
explanation: First and second generation Afro- Caribbean migrants to the UK have increased rates of psychotic illnesses (Mallett et al., 2002; Fearon et al., 2006; Selten et al., 2007). They are more likely to receive depot antipsychotics, and are less likely to be prescribed second- generation antipsychotics. The rates of schizophrenia in Caribbean countries are no higher than the incidence rates for the native White people in Britain, suggesting that genetic predisposition alone cannot account for the high reported rates of schizophrenia in African Caribbeans in the UK. In general, apart from the cultural influence on the content of delusions, the psychopathological features of schizophrenia do not differ notably among various patient groups. (Ref: Chaudhry et al., 2008 Journal of Psychopharmacology 22(6)673-680)

stem: In developmental psychology, the term symbiosis refers to which of the following phenomena?
options: The dual entity of father and mother
The dual entity of mother and caregiver
The dual entity of mother and the infant
The dual entity of twin siblings
The dual entity of brother and sister
correctAnswer: The dual entity of mother and the infant
explanation: Margaret Mahler proposed a theory to describe how young children acquire a sense of identity separate from that of their mothers’. During symbiosis (age 2-5 months), mother- infant is perceived as a single fused entity.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 892-893.

stem: The mother of an autistic child wants to know why her son lacks empathy for other children. Which of the following concepts might best explain the fundamental defect?
explanation: ‘Theory of mind’ refers to people’s intuitive understanding of their own and other people’s minds or mental states, including beliefs and thoughts. It develops by degrees from a very early age in humans: by the age of 3 years children normally have a well-developed theory of mind but cannot yet understand that people’s beliefs can be false. This develops around 4 years of age. People with autistic spectrum disorder are severely impaired in their ability to understand mental states and to appreciate how mental states govern behaviour.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

stem: When a mother leaves an infant, the infant can become upset. To compensate and comfort for this sense of loss, an object with the attributes of the mother is required. Winnicott called this object
explanation: Winnicott developed the notion of the transitional object. Ordinarily a pacifier, blanket, or teddy bear, this object serves as a substitute for the mother during infants’ efforts to separate and become independent. It provides a soothing sense of security in the absence of the mother.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1089.

stem: From the matching items, identify the incorrectly matched correspondence between mother's AAI (Adult attachment interview) category and infant's SSP behaviour pattern (strange situation procedure).
explanation: There is an 80% correspondence between a mother's attachment category on the AAI and her infant's attachment pattern. This indicates that a mother's care-giving behaviour towards her child is significantly influenced by her own attachment experience. Studies have shown that mothers in the dismissing adult attachment category typically have children who exhibit an avoidant attachment pattern, mothers in the pre-occupied/ entangled adult attachment category typically have children who exhibit a resistant attachment pattern, and mothers with unresolved attachment tend to have children with disorganised or disorientated attachment pattern.

stem: Which of the following descriptions is suggestive of dissocial personality disorder?
explanation:
A callous lack of concern for others, irresponsibility, irritability, aggression, tendency to act outside social norms, a disregard for the feelings of others, inability to maintain enduring

relationships, low threshold for violence, a tendency to blame others, evidence of childhood conduct disorder are the reported features of dissocial personality.

stem: ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for dissocial personality disorder includes:
explanation:
ICD-10 diagnostic criteria include:

a callous lack of concern for the feelings of others

an incapacity to maintain (not establish) enduring relationships

an incapacity to experience guilt

a persistent proneness to blame others

disregard for social norms

a very low frustration tolerance

Conduct disorder during childhood and adolescence, though not invariably present, may further support the diagnosis. Persistent irritability may be an associated feature.

stem: Regarding 'Quality Of Life-16', which of the following is true:
options: It cannot be used in patients with chronic illnesses
explanation:
Flanagan's QOLS originally had 15 items, but was expanded to include a 16th item

(independence). It measures five conceptual domains of quality of life:

1. material and physical well-being

2. relationships with other people

3. social, community and civic activities

4. personal development and fulfilment

5. recreation

It is most often used in samples with chronic illnesses. The QOLS is usually self- administered. It can also be completed by interview format. The QOLS can be completed in about 5 minutes. Scores can range from 16 to 112.
reference: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC269997/

stem: Charles Bonnet syndrome is associated with
explanation: Charles Bonnet syndrome: Elderly patients, with normal consciousness and no brain pathology, with reduced visual acuity due to ocular problems, experience vivid, distinct, usually well-coloured (in contrast to real sensation that is blurred due to eye disease) formed hallucinations – mostly humans, at times animals and cartoons. These objects usually show movement, and can be voluntarily controlled – disappear on closing the eyes; insight about unreality is usually preserved – though they may evoke emotions including fear and joy. About 1/3rd are elementary; usually the hallucinations are located in external space.

stem: Paramnesia is associated with
explanation: Reduplicative paramnesia involves the belief that a person, a place, or an event around one have been copied exactly. Capgras syndrome involves a belief that the patients' acquaintances (especially close relatives) are replaced with exact look-alikes. Thus Capgras delusion is considered to be one variant of the paramnesia of reduplication.

stem: Iconic memory lasts for
explanation: Iconic memory holds stimuli for up to a second. As a consequence, the flow of visual information seems smooth and continuous. The memory traces of auditory stimuli can last for several seconds, many times longer than the traces of visual stimuli. Iconic memory (or iconic store) is one of the sensory registers, allowing a visual image to persist for about half a second (depending on brightness) after a stimulus has ceased. It enables television, which presents 25 still images per second, each given twice to raise the flicker rate to 50 per second, to convey the illusion of a single continuous image which can be perceived as a moving image.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

stem: A forensic investigator tries to reconstruct the crime scene and encourages the witnesses to visit the scene of crime to aid this process. Which recall phenomenon is being utilized by this investigator?
explanation: Context-dependent memory is a form of state-dependent memory associated with the context in which information is learned and recalled. In a frequently-cited British experiment on context-dependent memory, lists of words that were learned by divers while they were underwater were best recalled when they were again underwater, and conversely words learned on land were best recalled on land.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

stem: John loves to gamble using slot machines in the casinos. The reinforcement achieved using slot machines is a type of
explanation: In operant conditioning, a variable-ratio schedule is one in which a reward is delivered after the organism has made a random number of responses, and is then rewarded after a further random number of responses, and so on. Ratio schedules, especially variable ratio schedules, can generate high rates of behaviour, as seen in the behaviour directed at a casino slot machine.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1018.

stem: The Thematic Apperception Test is a projective test of
explanation: The thematic apperception test is a projective personality test. It consists of a series of 10 black-and-white pictures that depict individuals of both sexes and of different age groups, who are involved in a variety of different activities. The stories that the patient makes up concerning the pictures, according to the projective hypothesis, reflect the patient’s own needs, thoughts, feelings, stresses, wishes, desires, and views of the future.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 59-60.

stem: A gentleman gets his pay cheque on the first day of every month. His salary provides which one of the following types of reinforcement?
explanation: A fixed-interval schedule is when behaviour is rewarded after a set amount of time. This type of schedule exists in payment systems when someone is paid hourly, weekly or monthly: no matter how much work that person does in one hour, week or month (behaviour), they will be paid the same amount (reinforcement). In operant conditioning, a fixed-interval schedule is a simple reinforcement schedule in which reward follows the first response that the organism makes after a predetermined time interval, and then the first response that it makes after the same interval, and so on.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

stem: Dr. Lepage is a GP who gets extra payments for every additional hour of clinical work that he undertakes. This reinforcement schedule is an example of
explanation: With a fixed-ratio schedule, there are a set number of responses that must occur before the behaviour is rewarded. In this example, the doctor earns extra money for every extra hour of clinic he does (interval is fixed). Fixed ratios are better suited to optimize the quantity of output, whereas a fixed interval can lead to a higher quality of output. In operant conditioning, a fixed-interval schedule is a simple reinforcement schedule in which reward follows the first response that the organism makes after a predetermined time interval, and then the first response that it makes after the same interval, and so on.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

explanation: In serial learning, the primacy effect is a tendency for the items near the beginning of the series to be better recalled than those near the middle.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015.

stem: The Tarasoff case was related to
explanation: On 27 October 1969, Tatiana Tarasoff was killed by her ex-boyfriend (Mr. P), who had previously declared his intentions during an appointment with his psychotherapist at the University of California at Berkley. The therapist notified the campus police, both orally and in writing, that the patient was dangerous and should be committed. Concerned about the breach of confidentiality, the therapist’s supervisor vetoed the recommendation and ordered all records related to the patient’s treatment destroyed. At the same time, the campus police temporarily detained Mr. P, but then released him. Two months later, Mr. P killed Tatiana. Her parents sued the university, and the Supreme Court ultimately decided that physicians and therapists have a duty to warn third parties of threatened danger arising from a patient’s violent intentions. As a final statement, the Court stated that ‘protective privilege ends where public peril begins.’
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 970. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 839.

stem: The double-bind theory in schizophrenia refers to
options: Migration being a precipitant for psychosis
Lack of motivation to remain abstinent from cocaine use
Giving contradictory messages to a child
One parent assumes a dominant and the other a submissive role
Parents downgrading the roles of each other
correctAnswer: Giving contradictory messages to a child
explanation: Gregory Bateson and Donald Jackson formulated the double bind concept. It was used to describe a hypothetical family, in which children receive conflicting parental messages about their behaviour, attitude and feelings. According to Bateson's hypothesis, children withdraw into a psychotic state to escape the unsolvable confusion of the double bind. Ref: Bateson, G., Jackson, D.D., Haley, J. and Weakland, J., 1956. Toward a theory of schizophrenia. Behavioral science, 1(4), pp.251-264.
